title: Building reasoning models from scratch with Python and PyTorch
excerpt: Eight videos and over 11 hours of code walk you through evaluation, scaling, reinforcement learning and distillation for a pre-trained Qwen3 model.
body:
A pre-trained Qwen-3 model is loaded, then reasoning methods are added in Python and PyTorch. The eight-video series walks through evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, totalling more than 11 hours of hands-on coding. Early chapters run on a CPU, while later fine-tuning benefits from a GPU. By the end of the series, a complete reasoning engine can be built from a modest LLM seed.

Readers will come away with a concrete understanding of how reasoning models extend conventional LLMs, how to scale inference, how to apply RL and distillation, and which hardware setups make the workflow practical.

## Reasoning models as upgraded LLMs  

The videos start with a small pre-trained Qwen-3 model and treat it as the engine. Post-training steps, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and optional inference-scaling tricks, are layered on top. This upgrade makes the model better at math, code, and other complex tasks. The source notes that most current-generation LLMs already expose a reasoning mode, meaning they internally incorporate similar upgrades.

## Evaluation and inference-time scaling  

Evaluation begins with simple text-generation checks on the CPU. The notebooks show how to measure token-level accuracy, compute loss, and compare against ground-truth answers.  

Inference scaling builds on that foundation. Techniques such as dynamic-length sampling, batch-wise generation, and cache-based reuse are implemented in PyTorch. The snippet below illustrates how the generation loop can be tweaked to trade latency for quality:

```python
def generate(model, prompt, max_len=128, temperature=0.7, device="cpu"):
    input_ids = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to(device)
    output = model.generate(
        input_ids,
        max_new_tokens=max_len,
        temperature=temperature,
        do_sample=True,
        pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id,
    )
    return tokenizer.decode(output[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
```

Changing `max_new_tokens` or `temperature` lets learners experiment with speed-quality trade-offs without rewriting core logic.

## Reinforcement learning from scratch  

Reinforcement learning (RL) is the second major post-training step. The course uses a verifiable reward signal, correctness on a set of math or coding problems, to fine-tune the Qwen-3 base. The RL loop is built from scratch in PyTorch, showing the policy-gradient update and reward normalization.  

The videos cover these RL components:

- Reward function that returns 1 for a correct answer, 0 otherwise  
- Log-probability extraction from the model’s output distribution  
- Advantage calculation by subtracting a moving-average baseline  
- Gradient ascent step using `optimizer.step()`

These steps make the reasoning model explicitly learn to prefer correct solutions over random guesses.

## Distillation of the RL-enhanced model  

After RL, distillation creates a smaller student model that mimics the RL-enhanced teacher. The loss is the KL-divergence between their output distributions. The series walks through the data pipeline, loss formulation, and training schedule. The result is a lighter model that retains most of the reasoning capability while running faster at inference time.

## Practical hardware tips and prerequisites  

The early text-generation and evaluation notebooks are designed to run on any laptop, making the entry point accessible. When the course reaches RL fine-tuning and distillation, a CUDA-enabled GPU becomes important to keep training times reasonable. The author points out that GPU acceleration reduces epoch time from hours to minutes, so the later videos recommend a GPU.  

A practical tip is to start with the CPU examples, verify correctness, then switch the same PyTorch code to a GPU by setting `device = "cuda"` and calling `.to(device)` on tensors. This pattern lets learners transition smoothly without rewriting core logic.  

The only prerequisites are comfort with Python and PyTorch; deep-learning framework expertise is not required. Access to a CPU suffices for the first two videos, while a GPU is needed for later fine-tuning. The *Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)* book and videos are recommended but not mandatory.

## The takeaway  

Reasoning models are essentially LLMs that have been post-trained with RL and optional inference scaling. Starting from a pre-trained Qwen-3 model, the course adds evaluation, scaling, RL, and distillation in Python and PyTorch, yielding a complete reasoning engine. Early steps run on a CPU, but GPU acceleration is needed for later training phases. Following the videos gives a hands-on path from a vanilla LLM to a production-ready reasoning model.
